units.title: Which database for a web app
units.summary: For a typical web app on one or a few servers, the choice turns on concurrent writes, how many machines talk to the database, and data size.

claims.text: SQLite is an embedded library, not a client/server engine.

refs.quote: SQLite does not compete with client/server databases. SQLite competes with fopen().
But SQLite is built into the application.
SQLite does not compete with client/server databases. SQLite competes with fopen().

units.title: SQLite
units.summary: An in-process library: one file, no server. Unlimited readers, one writer at a time; comfortable for most low-to-medium traffic sites.

claims.text: Fewer than 100K hits/day should work fine, a conservative estimate.

refs.quote: any site that gets fewer than 100K hits/day should work fine with SQLite
The 100K hits/day figure is a conservative estimate, not a hard upper bound.

claims.text: Unlimited readers, one writer at any instant.

refs.quote: SQLite supports an unlimited number of simultaneous readers, but it will only allow one writer at any instant in time.
any site that gets fewer than 100K hits/day should work fine with SQLite

units.title: PostgreSQL
units.summary: A client/server engine with multiversion concurrency: readers and writers never block each other, no database size limit, and extensible types and functions.

claims.text: Reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading.

refs.quote: reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading

claims.text: Database size is unlimited; a single relation tops out at 32 TB by default.

refs.quote: relation size 32 TB with the default BLCKSZ of 8192 bytes
reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading

units.title: What each choice costs
units.summary: SQLite gives up concurrent writers and network access; PostgreSQL asks you to run and look after a server.

claims.text: Many clients over a network should use a client/server engine.

refs.quote: If there are many client programs sending SQL to the same database over a network, then use a client/server database engine instead of SQLite.

claims.text: Client/server engines are designed for an attended datacenter.

refs.quote: Client/server database engines are designed to live inside a lovingly-attended datacenter at the core of the network.

claims.text: Running PostgreSQL means operating a database server: backups, upgrades, connections.

refs.quote: If there are many client programs sending SQL to the same database over a network, then use a client/server database engine instead of SQLite.

units.title: Verdict for one app server
units.summary: With one app server and modest writes, SQLite is enough and simpler; add a second app server or heavy concurrent writes and PostgreSQL is the safer choice.

claims.text: Busy, write-intensive or multi-server sites should consider client/server.

refs.quote: But if the website is write-intensive or is so busy that it requires multiple servers, then consider using an enterprise-class client/server database engine instead of SQLite.

claims.text: The recommendation depends on the stated context and is a judgement.
